title: Ancient Theories of Freedom and Determinism

summaries.example: Imagine you are deciding whether to study for a test. Aristotle might say your choice matters because what you do can help shape what happens next. A Stoic might say the whole chain of events is already part of fate, but your studying is still an important cause of a good result. Epicurus would say the future is not completely fixed, so your choice can make a difference.
summaries.summary: Ancient Greek philosophers studied freedom in two connected ways. First, they asked whether people can think about the future and make it turn out differently. A fatalist argument claimed that every future statement is already true or false. If that were so, it might seem that every future event is unavoidable and planning is pointless. Aristotle and Epicurus reject this conclusion in different ways. Aristotle says some future statements are not yet true or false. Epicurus agrees and also argues against a fully determined universe by proposing a small, unplanned movement of atoms called the swerve. Carneades accepts that future statements are true or false, but says truth does not cause an event. Our decisions can still be causes of what happens. The Stoics accept both truth about the future and causal determinism. They argue that our actions still matter because events can be linked together: seeking help can be part of the cause of getting better. Ancient thinkers also asked when people are responsible. Aristotle connects responsibility with voluntary action, knowledge, character, and the ability to do otherwise. Epicurus says reason helps us shape our character. The Stoics say actions can be ours even when determined, because we respond to impressions through our own minds. Later thinkers, including Alexander and Plotinus, develop other accounts of choice, responsibility, and control.
key_ideas: Ancient philosophers asked whether people can guide their actions and whether they deserve praise or blame.
A famous argument says that if future statements are already true or false, the future must already be fixed.
Aristotle says the future can be open and that our choices can help bring about different results.
Epicurus adds a tiny, chance movement of atoms called the swerve to oppose a completely fixed future.
The Stoics say everything has causes, but our own thinking and actions can still be part of how events happen.
The philosophers disagree about whether freedom requires being able to do something different.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas help us think about everyday questions: Can effort change what happens? When is a mistake really our fault? Does a person's past shape who they become? The ancient answers are different, but each tries to explain how people can be responsible and effective even in a world with causes, limits, and surprises. They also show that the modern phrase 'free will' does not capture every concern ancient philosophers had.

important_terms.definition: The idea that the future cannot be changed and that our choices cannot affect what happens.
The idea that every event is fixed by earlier causes, so only one future can happen.
Thinking carefully about what to do before acting.
An action that starts in a person's own thoughts, wishes, or decisions rather than being forced from outside.
The idea that a person is responsible only if they could have acted differently.

questions_to_think_about: If a future event is already true, does that mean it cannot be changed?
Can a choice matter if it has causes?
Should someone be blamed for an accident caused by something they did not know?
Is being free more about choosing between options or about acting according to good reasons?

summaries.example: Suppose you receive a difficult job offer and deliberate before accepting it. Aristotle would emphasize that deliberation is sensible only if more than one outcome is genuinely available, though his own view is not clearly a theory about causal determinism. Carneades would say that the truth of a future statement does not itself cause your decision; your voluntary mental activity can be a cause. A Stoic would say your decision is determined, yet still causally effective: the accepted offer occurs through your reasoning rather than independently of it. Alexander would reject the Stoic conclusion that you could not have chosen otherwise.
summaries.summary: The entry examines ancient debates about effective agency and moral responsibility rather than simply projecting the modern free-will problem backward. The first debate concerns fatalism. Arguments associated with Aristotle, Diodorus, and Cicero begin with the Principle of Bivalence: every statement, including a statement about tomorrow, is true or false. They then argue that an eternally true prediction makes its event necessary, so deliberation cannot affect anything. Aristotle rejects the fatalist conclusion and, on a standard interpretation, denies that bivalence applies to contingent future statements. Epicurus adopts a similar treatment of future statements, but also links bivalence with causal determinism and introduces the atomic swerve to prevent an inexorable chain of causes. The entry notes that the swerve's precise role in securing freedom is unclear. Carneades accepts bivalence but rejects the inference from truth to necessity. He distinguishes the fact that makes a statement true from the present causes of the event described. A future action may be true in advance without being caused by an immutable prior condition; a voluntary motion of the mind can therefore be both under our control and causally effective. The Stoics accept bivalence, causal determinism, and divine providence. Their notion of co-fated events says that an outcome may be fated together with the action through which it occurs. Deliberation is not pointless because the deliberation and its result are part of the causal route to the outcome. In discussions of responsibility, Aristotle emphasizes voluntary action, knowledge of circumstances, practical reason, character formation, and alternate possibilities. Epicurus also argues that reason enables people to reshape beliefs and character.¬¬
key_ideas: The fatalist argument moves from bivalence about future statements to the alleged inevitability of future events, but the crucial move from truth to necessity is disputed.
Aristotle commonly is interpreted as restricting bivalence for genuinely contingent future statements, while Epicurus rejects both bivalence and the Law of Excluded Middle for such cases.
Carneades retains bivalence and separates a statement's truthmaker from the causes that produce the event; voluntary mental motion can remain causally important.
The Stoics accept providential causal determinism but distinguish simple outcomes from co-fated outcomes, preserving the practical efficacy of deliberation.
Aristotle and Epicurus connect responsibility with character formation and reason, while the Stoics locate control in assent to impressions and reject the need for alternate possibilities.
Alexander develops an incompatibilist Aristotelian position; Plotinus treats freedom chiefly as rational mastery directed toward the good.
summaries.why_it_matters: The disagreements clarify several questions that are often run together: whether the future has a fixed truth value, whether events have sufficient causes, whether deliberation makes a difference, and whether responsibility requires alternative possibilities. They also show why unpredictability alone may not amount to freedom: a random event could reduce rather than increase control. Conversely, the Stoic position challenges the assumption that causal determination automatically makes action ineffective. Studying these arguments helps distinguish different meanings of 'freedom'—effective agency, responsibility, rational self-mastery, and the power to do otherwise.

important_terms.definition: The view that the future is inevitable and beyond our power to shape, often argued from claims about truth and future events.
The logical principle that every statement has exactly one truth value: true or false.
The thesis that sufficient prior causes fix every event that occurs.
A view that a future statement can be true because the event occurs, without that truth requiring present causes that make the event inevitable.
Epicurus's proposed occasional, undetermined deviation in atomic motion, intended to resist fatalism and a completely determined cosmos.
The claim that moral responsibility requires the agent to have been able to act otherwise.
The Stoic view that an event and the action that helps produce it can both be fated together.
The ancient idea of what is genuinely under an agent's control or depends on the agent.

questions_to_think_about: Does the truth of a future proposition require present causal conditions that guarantee its truth?
Would random events, such as Epicurus's swerve, provide control or merely add unpredictability?
Can an action be genuinely yours if it is determined, provided that it occurs through your reasoning and character?
Is the ability to do otherwise necessary for responsibility, or can responsibility depend on how an action proceeds from the agent?
Does deliberation need an open future, or can deliberation be effective as part of a determined causal process?

summaries.example: Imagine deciding whether to join a school club. You compare your choices and pick one. Aristotle would say this kind of planning makes sense because the future is not simply locked in. Epicurus would agree and say the world is not controlled by an unbreakable chain of causes. Carneades would add that even if it has always been true which club you will choose, that truth did not force you; your thinking and decision helped cause the choice. A Stoic would say your choice has causes, but your reasoning is still part of the cause, so planning was useful.
summaries.summary: Ancient philosophers explored freedom through two main questions. First, can people use thought and action to influence what happens? Second, when is it fair to praise or blame them? A famous fatalist argument begins with the Principle of Bivalence, the idea that every statement is true or false. If statements about tomorrow are already settled in this way, the argument says, then tomorrow's events must be unavoidable. Why plan or work for an outcome that must happen anyway? Aristotle answers that some future events are still open. Before a sea battle, for example, the statement that it will happen need not already be true or false in the same way as a statement about the past. Epicurus gives a similar response and also argues that nature is not one completely fixed chain. His theory includes the swerve, a small unpredictable movement of atoms. The source notes that it is not clear how this random movement would create responsible control. Carneades takes another route. He accepts that one future statement is true and its opposite false, but says that the truth of a statement does not force the event. A person's voluntary decision can still help cause what happens. The Stoics accept both future truth and causal determinism. They say that some outcomes happen no matter what, but other outcomes are linked with the actions that bring them about. Seeking treatment, for example, can be part of the cause of recovery. The Stoics therefore think deliberation can be useful even when it is itself caused. key_ideas: The ancient debate is about both making things happen and being responsible for what we do.
The fatalist argument says that fixed truth about the future would make effort and planning pointless.
Aristotle and Epicurus treat some future statements as not yet settled, while Carneades keeps the rule that they are already true or false.
The Stoics believe the universe is causally ordered, but they argue that our reasoning can still help produce events.
Aristotle and Epicurus say our repeated choices help form our character, which helps explain responsibility.
The Stoics reject the need to have chosen the opposite action; Alexander argues that this ability is necessary.
summaries.why_it_matters: These debates help separate ideas that are easy to confuse. A future event might be predictable without being caused by a prediction. An action might have causes without being forced from outside. And an unpredictable event might not be under anyone's control. The ancient theories also connect freedom with habits, reasoning, and responsibility, not only with making a choice at one instant. Their questions still matter whenever we ask whether effort makes a difference or how people should be held accountable.

important_terms.definition: The belief that the future is already unavoidable and that our actions cannot change it.
A rule in logic saying that every statement is either true or false.
The idea that earlier causes make one outcome necessary.
Careful thinking about different choices and their likely results.
An action that comes from the person's own thoughts and desires, rather than outside force.
The claim that responsibility requires being able to choose a different action.
Something that depends on an agent's own control or decision.
Epicurus's proposed tiny, unplanned movement of an atom, meant to prevent everything from being fixed by earlier causes.

questions_to_think_about: If you know something will happen, does your knowledge make it happen?
Can planning be useful in a world where every event has a cause?
Should a person be blamed for an action done by force or without knowing an important fact?
Do repeated choices help create the kind of person we become?
Would a random change in your brain make you more free or less in control?
